description: We are building an astrophysics-focused team for NASA Space Apps 2026, working on the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. Our goal is to develop an interactive web application that analyzes SPHEREx infrared sky observations and identifies changes in celestial objects over time. We are looking for motivated teammates interested in astrophysics, Python, AI/ML, data science, web development, and data visualization.
summary: Cosmic Lens is a public web tool for exploring NASA SPHEREx infrared images and seeing how the sky changes over time. Users pick two observations of the same sky region and compare them with three views: Blink (flips between the images), Slider (reveals one over the other), and Changes (highlights candidate differences in brightness and lists them). SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months in 102 near-infrared bands, far more data than anyone can inspect by hand. Cosmic Lens makes that data easy for students, amateur astronomers, and researchers to compare visually. This is a working prototype demonstrated on the galaxy M101.
details:
What it does: Cosmic Lens loads two SPHEREx observations of the same sky region and lets users flip between them (Blink), reveal one over the other (Slider), or highlight candidate changes in a clickable list (Changes).

How it works: We retrieved SPHEREx Level 2 spectral image cutouts of M101 (detector D2) from NASA/IPAC IRSA, subtracted the modeled zodiacal light, reprojected the later image onto the earlier image's sky grid, and normalized both. The web app then flags regions where normalized brightness differs beyond an adjustable sensitivity threshold.

Benefits and impact: It lowers the barrier for anyone, from students to researchers, to look for changes in a huge infrared survey, with no software to install.

Limitations: The two cutouts (weeks 2025W20 and 2026W21, about 1.54 and 1.56 micrometers) differ slightly in wavelength, SPHEREx pixels are about 6 arcseconds, and candidates near image borders are reprojection artifacts. M101 is a static target, so this prototype demonstrates the pipeline rather than a discovery. Flagged regions are candidates, not confirmed changes.

Future goals: Cover more sky regions, match wavelengths between observations, track moving objects such as comets and asteroids, and cross-match with Gaia DR3.

Tools: Python, Astropy, Astroquery, Reproject, NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib (data preparation); HTML, CSS and JavaScript (web app); GitHub Pages (hosting).

AI disclosure: An AI assistant helped write and debug parts of the code and polish the English text. The idea, challenge choice, and data decisions were ours.
